item.title: Is Taking Time Off to Play Video Games Really Problematic?
item.description:
Burnout

Is Taking Time Off to Play Video Games Really Problematic?

A planned day off for a new game release can help protect against burnout.

Posted November 5, 2026

Key points
  • Burnout typically comes from chronic ongoing workplace stress that has not been managed or mitigated.
  • Gaming on a planned day off can be a reasonable way to step away from work and recover before burnout sets in.
  • Video games can pose a very real problem for people who gravitate toward escapism and avoidance.

November brings two highly anticipated video game releases: the remake of "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time" and "Grand Theft Auto VI," arguably the most anticipated video-game release of all time. In the months leading up to these releases, news coverage has described employers planning around expected absences as some employees take time off just to play these games on release. The reaction to this notion from much of the general public has been disapproval, but I would argue that this disapproval is misplaced. Taking planned time off for an activity a person enjoys is not the lapse in responsibility it is perceived as, and can in fact be helpful in promoting mental wellness.

What is burnout?

Burnout is a syndrome of mental exhaustion, emotional distance, or cynicism toward one’s job, and reduced professional effectiveness. It typically comes from chronic ongoing workplace stress that has not been effectively managed or mitigated. The idea is that work generates fatigue that an individual would normally recover from. Over time, this fatigue intensifies, and the recovery is no longer sufficient, causing the individual to start the next day at a deficit that compounds over months. It starts to bleed through into other areas of life, like relationships, social engagement, and general wellness.

It is problematic because it will continue until the underlying stressors are more effectively managed or reduced, and the syndrome correlates with other health concerns like depression, insomnia, anxiety, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes.

What improves burnout?

Three approaches have provided the most consistent evidence for reducing burnout.

The first is changing the work structure itself. Interventions like reducing workload, increasing staffing, adjusting schedules, and improving teamwork have all shown reductions in burnout. This is a systems approach and not necessarily something within the control of the individual.

The second thing that improves burnout is individual stress management. This includes mindfulness training, stress-management programs, and small group collaboration.

The third approach is psychological detachment from work outside of work hours. Being able to deliberately turn off the “work brain” and focus on the “home brain” is associated with less exhaustion and better overall well-being.

How does this apply to gaming?

The last approach—being able to mentally detach from work—is generally accomplished through taking time off. However, not all time off leads to recovery. For recovery to occur, the time off needs to result in mental disengagement from work; it must involve some sort of activation energy; it must be relaxing; and it must be a decision within an individual’s control.

This blog is generally focused on using popular culture and video games in ways that can be productive and supportive for mental health management. I would posit that choosing to take a day off to play a video game that makes you excited is really just a deliberately timed vacation that has the potential to result in recovery.

Taking a day off to play "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time" not only brings excitement and anticipation, an emotionally healthy experience; it also provides mental disengagement from ongoing stressors, replacing those stressors with a positive experience in a deliberate fashion. Choosing to take a day off to play a video game is no different than taking a “mental health day” or pre-scheduling a long weekend for vacation.

The real concern is whether or not this type of behavior is akin to avoidance. Video games can pose a very real problem for people who gravitate toward escapism and avoidance. However, escapism and avoidance are typically reactive behaviors. Planning a day off ahead of time is a proactive behavior. This distinction realistically comes down to the timing. Is the gamer taking the day off at the last second because they’d rather play the game instead of fulfilling their obligations, or is this a deliberate and planned activity? The latter could be seen as a healthy habit and a preventative option to protect against burnout; the former, a symptom of burnout itself.

Gaming on a planned day off can be a reasonable way to step away from work and recover before burnout sets in. If the time away doesn’t help, the stressors driving the burnout likely need to be addressed directly.

item.title: What Happens to Good Memories After Family Estrangement?
item.description:
Memory

What Happens to Good Memories After Family Estrangement?

Personal Perspective: Estrangement doesn't require us to give up memories of when we felt loved.

Posted November 5, 2026

Source: Daniela Dimitrova / Pixabay

One of my fondest memories of my father is the night he taught me how to write my name.

I was little, sitting at a Fisher-Price table with a new arts-and-crafts set, drawing with crayons. My mother had gone to bed. I think my father had gone in to check on her or say good night, leaving me sitting at the little table by myself.

When he came back out, I proudly showed him what I had written on my paper: “Look, I wrote my name!” I remember exclaiming proudly. I had written the letters “K.T.” on a paper with pink crayon.

"KT." A little girl’s phonetic attempt at spelling my actual name, "Kaytee."

“Let me show you how to spell it,” I remember him saying with a smile. It was just him and me, late at night. It was probably much earlier than I remember, but in my mind it was dark and late, long past when a little girl should have been awake, making it extra exciting. The world was ours. He took a crayon and wrote: K-A-Y-T-E-E across a clean, crisp piece of white craft paper. It was like a new world had opened. That was the night I learned how to write (and spell!) my name.

At least, that’s how I remember it. I’m in the first year of my 40s now, remembering something that happened when I was a very young child. I know memory doesn’t work like a video recording. Details fade. Our minds fill in spaces. Maybe it wasn’t a pink crayon; maybe it was green. Maybe some of the details happened differently than I remember them. Sometimes I even wonder if the whole thing was a dream, or a story I somehow created for myself over the years.

But I don’t think so. And, if I’m being truthful, I don’t really want to know. Because it is one of my fondest memories of my father.

I often say that it would be easier, in some ways, if every memory were bad. If I could look backward and find nothing worth missing. Nothing that makes me wonder how the person in that memory could possibly be the same person who would someday choose not to know me.

Maybe that’s part of what makes my abandonment so difficult. For a long time, I think I believed I needed to understand how those two truths fit together. I needed an explanation for how the father sitting beside me with the pink crayon, his 6'2" frame barely fitting as he crouched beside the plastic Fisher-Price craft table, became the father who has refused to speak to me for 15 years. I don’t think I’m going to get one.

I like believing that it happened exactly that way: There was once a little girl sitting at a Fisher-Price table with a crayon in her hand, trying to write her name. And in my memory, her father sat down beside her and showed her how.

item.title: Tips for Setting Boundaries With Family During the Holidays
item.description:
Boundaries

Tips for Setting Boundaries With Family During the Holidays

A guide for handling difficult family conversations.

Posted November 5, 2026

Key points
  • Set boundaries by identifying what you will do, rather than setting rules for others.
  • Use kind, clear language that assumes good intentions.
  • If boundaries are disregarded, use direct communication and concrete boundary management strategies.
Source: cottonbro studio / Pexels

With the holidays quickly approaching, the influx of family gatherings is right around the corner. If you've avoided certain relatives and are growing anxious about the idea of being stuck next to them at the dinner table, now is the time to learn how to set boundaries.

The intention behind setting and maintaining boundaries is not to push people away, create distance, or cut off relationships. Instead, boundaries communicate what we need to feel comfortable and maintain healthy, connected relationships with others. They help create the conditions for relationships to thrive, even when people have different perspectives or expectations.

When thinking about setting boundaries, it’s helpful to understand the difference between setting a rule and setting a boundary. A rule tells someone else what they can or cannot do ("You can't give me parenting advice"). Alternatively, a boundary identifies what you are willing to do ("If you continue to try and give me parenting advice, I'm going to step away from the conversation"). We cannot control what other people say, but we can control how we respond.

One helpful approach to navigating difficult family conversations during the holidays is through Melissa Urban's Green, Yellow, Red framework in The Book of Boundaries: Set the Limits That Will Set You Free.

The framework encourages people to consider the perceived threat a situation poses to their health, safety, or relationships and respond accordingly. Here are examples related to a relative repeatedly giving unsolicited parenting advice or criticizing your parenting choices:

  • Green (low threat): Use kind, clear language that assumes good intentions: "I appreciate you wanting to help, but we’ve already decided how we want to handle [issue]. This works for our family.”
  • Yellow (elevated threat): Be more direct when the relative disregards your boundaries or pushes back. For example: "I know you really love our kids and want what’s best for them. I understand you see this differently, but I’m not going to keep defending our parenting choices. Let’s move on. How is work going?"
  • Red (high threat): If the relative continues to disregard the boundary, it likely requires direct communication and concrete boundary management strategies. For example: "I’ve told you several times I’m not open to discussing this. I’m going to step away. I hope we can chat later about something else."

These situations can arise during family gatherings, particularly when grandparents or other relatives have strong opinions about how children should be raised. Sometimes, choosing to parent differently than your own parents can feel like criticism of their parenting choices. Instead, parents can acknowledge that relatives have their own experiences and perspectives while maintaining that parenting decisions belong to the parents.

Source: cottonbro studio / Pexels

In an earlier post, I outlined specific recommendations for new parents for developing and maintaining boundaries:

  1. Remember that you are responsible for setting and maintaining boundaries for your family. This includes establishing boundaries that protect your children's autonomy and how they interact with others.
  2. Start from a place of "we-ness" with your partner. Make sure you are on the same page so you can communicate your parenting decisions and boundaries as a team.
  3. Be direct and concise. You don't need to overexplain, justify, or defend. The more you try to convince someone, the more opportunity you give for debate.
  4. Ask for support without criticism. Instead of focusing only on what you don't want relatives to do, communicate what would be helpful. For example, "We'd really appreciate your support in following the routines we've established for the kids. Here’s how you can help…"
  5. Boundaries can be different for different people. Your boundaries may differ with grandparents, siblings, or other relatives depending on your relationship history, their behavior, and what you need to feel comfortable. That's OK!

item.title: Unintentional Intentions: When a Photo Tour Yields a Different Mindset
item.description:
Creativity

Unintentional Intentions: When a Photo Tour Yields a Different Mindset

Personal Perspective: Taking a photo with intention can teach you to observe more closely.

Posted November 5, 2026

Key points
  • Learning can lead to unexpected, and often great, outcomes.
  • Photography can be a way to change our thinking.
  • Unintentional accident (in photography) might be a road to becoming more intentional in life.

Since one of my goals is to keep learning, I am trying something new this autumn. And sometimes that lets me smash my thinking, change my views, and maybe my behavior. I had (partial) success recently when I went on a photography workshop/tour in Vietnam.

I’ve worked in Hanoi for decades, so I know it well. I’ve seen remarkable economic change—some people describe it as going from “from bicycles to Bentleys.” And, I’ve been there long enough to know people who have married, had children, lost spouses, and had grandchildren.

The photo tour appealed to me for two reasons. First, I could see and learn about other intriguing parts of the country, from the south (Ho Chi Minh City) to the central area (the arts community of Hoi An, the ancient capital of Hue), and the world-class caves of Phong Nha. And someone else would organize it all.

Lunch in the market
Source: N.K.Napier

My second reason for going was to learn how to “see differently, like photographers.” I went as a writer, not a photographer, but joined people who are (nearly) professionals. They showed up with their 20-plus pounds of fabulous gear, and I showed up with my iPhone camera. No question I would learn from them.

Off we went.

The learning about techniques part was straightforward, mainly because of the photography instructor.

She was phenomenally skilled and refreshingly nonjudgmental. She worked with each of us wherever we were in our photo journeys. She helped us with equipment, technique, and how to shape and create a photo. She taught me about the iPhone (and admitted that she has transitioned from a big camera to the iPhone as her main piece of gear!). I learned about new (to me) photo approaches, like ICM. At the first showing of our photos, everyone was going on about ICM. I’ve never been shy about asking the “dumb question,” so I admitted I had no idea what they were talking about.

“Intentional camera movement,” four people said at once.

My translation: blurry photos that can look like multiple exposures in a single frame, but done with intention instead of as a mistake. The person who used ICM took gorgeous images that danced with color.

By the end of the tour, I decided I was doing U-ICM—un-intentional camera movement—and got lucky with some of the photos that turned out to be interesting.

Unintentional camera movement that worked!
Source: N.K.Napier

So I did learn about photography and how others looked at a scene and shaped it. But the biggest lesson, now that I look back, was my mindset change.

Taking a photo with intention forced me to slow down, observe closely (foreground, background in addition to the main area of focus), and, as the instructor would say, “think about what feeling or idea you want to convey.”

So, that’s what I’m trying to do.

I have a long way to go, but my goal is to do this every day for at least 5 to 10 minutes: slow down, choose a scene, and think about how to frame it. Then shoot.

I’ll keep you posted.

item.title: How Books Can Boost Emotional Intelligence
item.description:
Emotional Intelligence

How Books Can Boost Emotional Intelligence

Author Sandra V. Feder on the "Emotions and Me" series of picture books.

Posted November 5, 2026

Key points
  • When children see their experiences reflected in books, those experiences become validated and normalized.
  • Picture books are wonderful conversation starters because they’re meant to be read together.
  • Giving our children the gift of powerful words and of our attention is vitally important.

Reading to your child can not only improve their early literacy skills, which are important for later academic achievement, but it can also boost their emotional intelligence.

Choosing the right books to read with your child can build emotional intelligence, teaching them about feelings, helping them to become more aware of their thoughts, and modeling important skills for managing big emotions. When characters in the story experience the daily challenges and accompanying feelings that your child faces, they receive validation and empathy in the pages of the book, and in your warm presence as you read to them a story that feels personal.

Author Sandra V. Feder has worked to intentionally bring children’s emotions to the page through her Emotions and Me series of books, tackling big feelings that kids experience like loneliness, anger, and shyness, so that children can feel seen and validated, and build emotional intelligence for the future.

Q: Share a bit about your background and what inspired you to write the Emotions and Me series of picture books.

Author Sandra V. Feder has worked to intentionally bring children’s emotions to the page through her "Emotions and Me" series of books.
Source: Groundwood Books/Used with permission

Sandra V. Feder: I’ve been a writer my whole life, from an early career in print journalism to becoming a children’s book author, so I am always thinking about how we use words. When I had children of my own, it seemed natural to talk about words we use to describe feelings, because all kids have lots of big feelings.

My inspiration for the Emotions and Me series, which includes Angry Me, Peaceful Me, Shy Me, and Lonely Me, was my youngest daughter’s anger. Trying to understand what she was feeling led me to explore situations, whether at home, school, or out in the world, that contributed to her anger. I chose to write this series in relatable first-person voices to validate children’s feelings and frustrations. Each book also offers ways children can help soothe themselves and learn strategies to help with emotions.

Q: What role can books play in helping children to learn about emotions and self-regulation?

Sandra V. Feder: Books can be hugely important in a child’s understanding of their own emotional life, including how to explain and manage feelings. When young children see their experiences reflected in books, those experiences become validated and normalized, helping them feel less alone in navigating whatever it is they’re feeling.

Each of the books in the series deals with a different emotion and describes familiar scenarios when a child might experience that emotion. The books give children agency—there’s a point in each book where the child tries to find solutions. Those might include talking to a friend, asking for help, or putting words to the feeling even though it seems like no one will understand.

Picture books are wonderful conversation starters because they’re meant to be read together. That opens the door for meaningful discussions where the adult can ask the child guiding questions, allowing them both to share their experiences with similar feelings.

Q: From your experience as a parent and children’s book author, what three things can parents do to help children with their big feelings?

Sandra V. Feder: The most important thing is to talk about feelings. You have to be able to name it to tame it. Helping your children put words to their feelings is a gift. In Lonely Me, there is a scene where the child is feeling ignored by an older sibling on his phone. The lonely character remarks, “When I feel lonely, sometimes it helps to ask for attention,” and then adds, “No more screens!” Those simple words really empower a child. When my oldest daughter was young, and I was focused on her two younger sisters, I taught her to say, “I need a little attention.” I didn’t want her to fall apart just to get what she needed. In our current times, we’ve all felt the sting of someone paying more attention to a screen than to us. Giving our children the gift of powerful words and of our attention is vitally important.

Parents can also help their children simply by listening. All too often, adults brush aside a child’s feeling because it’s coming at an inconvenient time, like when we’re rushing out the door for school or trying to wind down at bedtime. But it’s important, even if we can’t do it right then, to circle back and make time to understand our children’s feelings. Sometimes what we see as anger might really be frustration, fatigue, or hurt feelings. Each of those requires a different response and a different path for regulation.

Finally, parents shouldn’t be afraid to share their own feelings. When children see that it’s okay to have strong emotions, it’s a powerful way to begin teaching them how to regulate those feelings. Explaining how we handle our own big feelings, like taking deep breaths when we’re angry or reaching out to friends when we’re feeling lonely, can be lovely teaching moments and allow parents to lead by example.

Source: Groundwood Books/Used with permission
Source: Groundwood Books/Used with permission

Q: How did you choose the emotions to focus on in the Emotions and Me series? How do loneliness, anger, peacefulness, and feeling shy resonate deeply with young readers?

Sandra V. Feder: I started with Angry Me, and I felt strongly that the main character be a girl, because girls and women often get the message that they shouldn’t feel anger. Angry Me has resonated very deeply with young readers, precisely because it explores such a universal emotion.

While I was working on that book, I realized I wanted to do a book that showed the opposite emotion, and I landed on peaceful. In Peaceful Me, the boy starts out talking about how he likes feeling peaceful and all the situations and places he does. But when a friend does something to jolt him out of that peaceful feeling, he shares the ways he tries to get back to it, like finding a hug, taking deep breaths, and remembering things that make him happy.

Tackling shyness came about because one of my own children had shy moments, even around people she knew well. In that story and in Angry Me, I didn’t want to imply that the feeling was wrong; rather, I wanted to acknowledge that it’s just one part of who we are. We can talk about it and learn ways to handle that shyness. It’s another feeling so many children experience, but it doesn’t need to be a defining or forever feeling.

Lonely Me, the newest book in the series, was inspired by my concern over the epidemic of loneliness in the United States and in other places around the world, which deeply affects our youth. Loneliness can arise from feeling different, experiencing loss, or when there’s a lack of meaningful connection, and the story provides ways to make connections and soothe that loneliness.

Source: Groundwood Books/Used with permission

Q: Why is children’s mental health so important, and how can parents lay a strong foundation for the next generation’s mental health and well-being?

Sandra V. Feder: Children’s mental health is vitally important. As they grow, the problems they confront—from social situations to challenges at school and at home—grow, too. Giving our children the tools they need to understand and talk about their feelings, and to begin to self-manage those feelings, sets them up for success.

My books promote social-emotional learning, including naming feelings, empathy, self-management, and relationship building. All of these are skills children need now and in the future.

Q: What do you hope young readers take away from spending time with your books?

Sandra V. Feder: I hope children feel seen in my books. I want them to learn new ways to talk about their feelings, to understand what might be underlying or causing those feelings, and to learn new tools for handling those feelings.

I hope my books help children appreciate the richness of their emotional lives, discover words to describe their feelings, and develop greater empathy for the emotional journeys of others.

item.title: Why Socrates Thought Us Fools
item.description:
Wisdom

Why Socrates Thought Us Fools

Why we would rather be wrong than be proved wrong.

Posted November 5, 2026

Key points
  • Socrates believed that our greatest problem is not knowing that we are ignorant.
  • We resist challenges to our beliefs because we experience them as attacks on our identity.
  • We are not merely ignorant; we are invested in remaining ignorant.
Socrates questioning the priest Euthyphro, who is in a hurry to leave.
Source: Neel Burton, AI-generated image.

In 399 BCE, the Athenians sentenced Socrates to death. His crime? He had spent his life making people look like the fools that they were.

Officially, Socrates was charged with impiety and corrupting the youth. For years, this eccentric septuagenarian had gone around asking people questions, exposing the inconsistencies and contradictions in their opinions. In his mind, he had been doing them the greatest favour.

Socrates had discovered something about human nature that remains as true today as it was in antiquity: Our problem is not so much that we are ignorant, but that we are ignorant of our ignorance.

The Wisest Man in Athens

According to his student Plato, Socrates had a friend called Chaerephon, who once travelled to Delphi and, on a whim, asked the oracle whether anyone was wiser than Socrates. The oracle replied in the negative: “There is no one wiser than Socrates.”

Socrates was as surprised and perplexed as everyone. He knew that he was not wise—but, surely, the god of the oracle could not have been mistaken? To find out what the god might have meant, he went around questioning people with a reputation for wisdom, beginning with the politicians, then the poets, and finally the craftsmen.

The politicians, he found, could not even explain the words that they were using. The poets wrote beautiful verses but struggled to make sense of them. The craftsmen possessed genuine expertise, but mistakenly assumed that this made them knowledgeable about everything else.

Socrates concluded that he was wiser than these supposedly wise men in one small but critical respect: He did not think he knew what he did not know.

The Trouble With Knowing Everything

From then on, Socrates devoted himself to questioning his fellow Athenians. He would ask a general to define courage, a priest to define piety, or a pair of good friends to define friendship. They would offer a confident answer, only for Socrates to expose some inconsistency or contradiction. He and they would then explore the concept in every direction until everyone threw up their hands in despair at their inability to define even the most important and apparently self-evident things.

This method of questioning, known as elenchus, or the Socratic method, aimed to bring about a state of puzzlement called aporia.

Aporia, if you like, is the honest and fertile state of knowing that you do not know.

One day, Socrates met a youth called Theaetetus, whose perplexity delighted him. Socrates said to him, “I see, my dear Theaetetus, that Theodorus had a true insight into your nature when he said that you were a philosopher, for wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.”

The Perils of Being Right

But there was a problem. As I discuss in my book, The Gang of Three, Socrates’ interlocutors did not want to be helped. Deep down, in a place unknown even to them, they did not welcome the truth.

Our beliefs are not merely propositions that we hold in our heads. They are bound up with our sense of who we are. To challenge a person’s beliefs is to challenge that person’s identity, standing, and meaning. We defend our beliefs as if we were defending ourselves.

Socrates understood this all too well. To prevent his interlocutors from getting angry or running away, he frequently feigned ignorance or used flattery. His approach rather resembles that of Lieutenant Columbo, the apparently bumbling detective who always has just one more question.

The Price of Wisdom

By exposing the ignorance of prominent Athenians, Socrates acquired admirers, especially among the young, but also powerful enemies.

At his trial, he reproached his fellow citizens for concerning themselves with wealth and reputation while neglecting wisdom, truth, and the proper care of their souls.

He compared himself to a gadfly attached by the gods to a great but listless horse: Athens needed him to sting her into wakefulness.

Even with his life at stake, Socrates refused to change his ways. If anything, he dropped the mask.

Socrates had spent his life showing people that they were fools. In condemning him, the Athenians demonstrated just how right he was.

And two-and-a-half thousand years later, what has changed? We still prefer certainty to doubt, reassurance to correction, and the appearance of wisdom to the difficult business of acquiring it.

We are not merely ignorant; we are invested in remaining ignorant.

For more, see The Ancient Technique That Changes Minds.

item.title: Between Stimulus and Response: The Space of Choice
item.description:
Persuasion

Between Stimulus and Response: The Space of Choice

Every day, we face countless moments of decision and choice.

Posted November 5, 2026

Key points
  • While circumstances undoubtedly influence us, they do not necessarily determine every response.
  • We have control of our thoughts, which indicates that we have control of our choices.
  • The action of not making a choice is still a choice, which will lead to consequences.
Source: Gerd Altmann / Pixabay

Every day presents countless moments of decision and choice. Some seem significant and some not. While circumstances also undoubtedly influence us, they do not necessarily determine every response. Between an event and a reaction lies a moment of choice. As Viktor Frankl, author of Man's Search for Meaning, observed: "Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose our response. In our response lies our growth and our freedom."

Profoundly, Frankl did not arrive at this conclusion while living a comfortable life. He made this observation while existing in circumstances where almost every external freedom had been removed. Yet he was somehow of the mind that one freedom remained—and that was the mind-based freedom to choose one's response.

It stands to reason that others can influence us, pressure us, provoke us, encourage us, or attempt to persuade us. Added to this, physical and social circumstances can also advance or constrain the options available to us. However, as noted by Frankl, we still have control of our thoughts, which indicates that we have control of our choices.

Questions of Blame

Consequently, this “space” (between stimulus and response) is also where the question of blame can—and does—arise. For example, expressions such as "It’s not my fault" or "I had no choice" are often considered familiar statements.

Here is what I believe we need to note: This almost incomprehensible insight and associated profound self-selected “mind-based power” of Frankl's statement, in which he declares that between stimulus and response there is a space, indicates—that in this now—self-selected “mind-based space”—there really is “something” immutably and “objectively and consciously extraordinary” taking place within the universal human condition. And with this insight taking place, Frankl concludes with the amazing declaration: “In that space is our power to choose our response. In our response lies our growth and our freedom."

As such, and further to this, Frankl infers and extrapolates that external pressure, provocation, and/or suppression will have an impact on the mind or anyone; however, according to Frankl, external circumstances cannot control thoughts, attitude, or choice.

This premise now extends into the unbelievable and extraordinary deep insight of Frankl, in which he declares that the space between stimulus and response is where self-selected and self-initiated choice takes place. What else can this insight suggest? To me, it suggests power, which the self owns and controls. However, what if the circumstances are such that there is no personal power over anything?

What then needs to be noted is that this capacity for choice—in this space between stimulus and response—is not a panacea for anything. So then, does choice actually exist? According to Frankl—who was in a position where he had no power over anything—between stimulus and response there was a space. As such, choices could be made. How is this at all possible? Yet, as the extraordinary experience and evidence of Frankl declares, it is possible.

Personal Ownership of Choices and Their Consequences

As such, when choices are made, consequences will take place, and with this we need to note that the action of not making a choice is still a choice, which will lead to consequences.

With this being the case, the question that must now be asked is: What do we do with this extraordinary, deep, and universally powerful insight by Frankl? One consideration is to understand that (irrespective of circumstances or time), in this space (between stimulus and response) where choice takes place, this choice belongs to the self, and it cannot be transferred to another person.

Consequently, to say, in terms of choices made, "It’s not my fault,” or "I had no choice"—these statements do not meet the test of the Categorical Imperative.

As Immanuel Kant points out, if every individual were permitted to transfer blame for a self-selected choice to another person by saying, “My road rage was not my fault,” or “I had no choice,” that would mean that accountability and personal responsibility—from a philosophical and social perspective—are not be universal ethical and moral principles (Kant, 1785/2012). However, the fact is that you are accountable and responsible for your choices, just the same as everyone else. And it is this universal truth that meets with the universality of the Categorical Imperative of Kant.

Following on from there, the next question that must also be asked is: Where to from here? And to this question, there is only one universal answer: Between stimulus and response there is space. It is you who must decide what that answer is.

item.title: AI-tiquette: When Did That Become Okay?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI-tiquette: When Did That Become Okay?

The strange new manners of a world in which effort is optional.

Posted November 5, 2026

Key points
  • Concealing AI assistance can feel deceptive; revealing it can diminish the message.
  • The signal of care can increasingly be produced independently of the experience and expenditure of care.
  • If everyone can generate elaborate outputs on demand, abundance may gradually drain them of value.
Source: Walther, AI-generated with ChatGPT / OpenAI, 2026

There was a time, not long ago, when asking a machine to write a birthday message would have seemed absurd. Having it compose a condolence note might have felt callous. Sending an artificial intelligence (AI)-written love letter? Surely that crossed a line. Using it to answer a colleague’s thoughtful email bordered on insulting. Now consider the same acts in 2026. From love life via friends to work, generative AI outputs have become all-pervasive. We may still hesitate, yet ever less. Behaviors that once provoked outrage are evolving through a familiar cycle: questionable becomes tolerated; tolerated becomes normal; and gradually normal becomes invisible.

Welcome to AI-tiquette: the rapidly evolving, largely unwritten etiquette governing what we delegate to AI, what we still believe deserves human effort, and how we judge one another as that boundary shifts.

From outrageous to ordinary

Social norms arise without trumpets. They morph and migrate as behaviors evolve, and contribute to that evolution. Answering a phone at the dinner table once signaled importance; eventually it was regarded as plain discourtesy. Texting instead of calling initially seemed impersonal; today, an unexpected phone call feels intrusive for many. AI accelerates the technological integration process—but it changes something more fundamental than the style in which we communicate. It moderates the amount of human effort behind the communication itself. That process is ongoing, and experiments involving email, texting, dating, and social media reveal how unstable our AI-tiquette is. Initially, many people failed to suspect AI involvement unless the possibility was explicitly raised (or the output was suspiciously spiked with AI-favorites like "profound" or "it is not...it is..."). Nowadays, AI is more and more taken for granted. Once its use is disclosed, however, judgments tend to become negative. Research identifies an “AI penalty,” as AI-mediated messages are perceived as less trustworthy and authentic.

AI-tiquette is a paradox. Concealing assistance can feel deceptive; revealing it can diminish the message. Most people simultaneously believe AI involvement ought to be disclosed, and do not disclose it.

Please, thank you, regenerate

Then there are our manners toward the machine. Do you say “please” to ChatGPT or "thank you" to Claude? Apologize when you change direction? Or type: “Wrong, redo. Shorter." Perhaps it does not matter to the machine. (And yet, politeness toward your bot may actually pay off. Research into human-AI information-seeking conversations suggests that impolite prompts can produce more language while yielding less useful information relative to the energy consumed.) The interesting question is whether it matters to us. Research following repeated human-AI interactions found that politeness toward AI deteriorated over time, and faster than in comparable human-to-human exchanges. Give the AI a more human-like presence and courtesy persists longer. Manners are messages to others, but they are also habits of the human producing them. If commanding, interrupting, and dismissing an infinitely patient artificial subordinate becomes something we practice hundreds of times a week, why assume the behavioral boundary will remain perfectly sealed around the machine?

The new insult: Outsourced attention

The deeper etiquette problem begins when another human being is at the other end. Imagine spending time to carefully craft an email to a colleague. She asks AI to summarize it and formulate a response. You receive three polished paragraphs and, pressed for time, ask your AI to summarize them. Two humans have now “communicated” without ever actually encountering what the other truly produced. Everything that is being written has been filtered. Was anyone rude? Your instinctive answer may be yes. Yet our inherited formal etiquette struggles because every visible feature of the exchange may be impeccable. The sentences are courteous, the grammar polished, the response prompt, the content professional. The potential discourtesy lies beneath the words: Attention has been withdrawn from the relationship while its appearance has been preserved. This withdrawal is now increasingly twice removed from humans, as AI agents are communicating on behalf of the sender/receiver.

The tension becomes sharper when emotion is involved. We still use effort as evidence of care. Yet even that norm is becoming porous. AI-assisted writing experiments indicate that people can produce messages perceived as warm and trust-building while spending considerably less time writing them. And research on emotionally engaging conversations suggests that AI-generated responses can produce strong feelings of interpersonal closeness when recipients believe another person wrote them. We are approaching a painful threshold: The signal of care can increasingly be produced independently of the experience and expenditure of care.

The lost bliss of friction

Human culture has long attached meaning to effort. A handwritten letter mattered partly because somebody sat down and wrote it. Generative AI removes much of it. Often that is valuable: It can bridge languages, clarify muddled thinking, overcome barriers, and help people articulate something genuinely felt. Yet friction was never merely an inconvenience. Sometimes it was part of how value was created. If everyone can generate elaborate proposals, comments, images, and responses on demand, abundance may gradually drain those outputs of informational and emotional value. The emerging breach of AI-tiquette may be surprisingly old-fashioned: wasting somebody else’s time. It is an exploit which we now master at industrial scale. In an attention-scarce environment, it is an insult that will backfire as our recipients will simply learn to ignore us.

The 4 "whys"

Rules about acceptable AI use will keep changing. Four questions along the way can serve us, and those who interact with us:

  1. Why do you use it? What does AI genuinely add—clarity, access, perspective, creativity, speed?
  2. Why should you skip it? Would doing this yourself exercise a capacity you want to retain, make you think, or communicate care that matters?
  3. Why are you producing this at all? When production becomes almost effortless, creation needs a stronger reason. Does this email, report, post, or image deserve to exist—and deserve someone else’s attention?
  4. And above all three lies the most important question: What is your why? When almost everything can be pursued with minimal effort, what are you passionate enough to create?

item.title: Why You Get Annoyed, and What to Do About It
item.description:
Self-Help

Why You Get Annoyed, and What to Do About It

Annoyance reveals when our capacity is low as our mind creates bigger stories.

Posted November 5, 2026

Key points
  • Hunger, poor sleep, heat, and stress can reduce our ability to respond patiently to everyday frustrations.
  • Research shows that our physical state influences emotions, social perception, and relationships.
  • The mind can amplify minor irritations by connecting them to past disappointments and perceived threats.
  • Recognizing our needs, questioning our stories, and choosing connection can help us respond better.

If you are annoyed, it’s not just about the annoying thing.

A few week ago, I was stuck in an airport trying to get to Washington, DC. It was Friday, and it had become one of those travel days that starts out inconvenient and then slowly turns into a nightmare: Two cancelled flights, and a long line of tired people trying to rebook.

I did not make it that night. I ended up taking a red-eye. But somewhere in the middle of this travel chaos, I was thinking about what word we should use in today's post. I jokingly thought: annoyance—and that is the one we landed on.

Annoyance is small. It is everyday. It is leaf blowers and people chewing loudly and your partner leaving his black socks on the floor again and your kid asking you where their shoes are while standing next to their shoes.

Annoyance is the emotional wallpaper of being human.

Annoyance Is Not Just About the Annoying Thing

The same person can annoy you on one day and not annoy you on another.

Your mother can say the exact same thing on Monday and you laugh, and then on Thursday she says it again and you want to leave the room.

So what changed?

Usually two things: Your capacity, and your story.

Capacity: How Much Room Do I Have Right Now?

Capacity is your bandwidth to be with life as it is, and is not just a mindset; it is biological. It’s impacted by heat, hunger, sleep, stress, hormones, and illness.

We joke about being "hangry," but it is real; there is research on hunger and irritability. When you are hungry, you are more likely to feel anger and irritation—and less likely to feel pleasure. Your body is saying, please feed me, and then your mind starts saying, everyone is terrible.

Sleep is another big one. Poor sleep changes your social perception. Couples that sleep poorly tend to have more conflict, less positive emotion, and less ability to accurately read each other.

It is an early warning signal.

Annoyance says, Check your capacity: Have I eaten? Am I too hot? Am I tired? Am I overloaded?

Because sometimes annoyance can be remedied with some protein or a good night’s rest.

How the Mind Turns an Incident Into a Whole Identity

An incident happens. Something small, like someone is late, doesn't respond to your text, or—if you are like me on that dreaded red-eye flight—you get stuck in the middle seat.

That is the incident. What fuels your annoyance is when your mind adds story to it. Your mind will pull in history and all the ways you have been disappointed before, the moments you didn't feel considered, and fuel the irritants like adding kindling to a fire.

Your mind can take an incident and turn it into a trend, an identity, or even a false truth: They never think about me. I am always the one who has to adjust. No one respects my time. I am trapped.

And then we are dealing with a whole elaborate story that feels real but is not true.

Annoyance Separates Us

When we are annoyed, we separate. We separate from reality, the present moment, or even the person right in front of us. We also separate from the fact that other people are also tired, hot, delayed, worried, trying, failing, needing a break, needing a snack, orneeding a little mercy.

This Week’s Practice: Work With Annoyance

Annoyance is a beautiful teacher because it arises in ordinary life. This week, do not try to get rid of annoyance. Instead, explore it.

1. Check capacity. Get out of your head and into your body: Am I hungry? Am I tired? Am I overstimulated? Do I need water, food, movement, quiet, or a break?

Sometimes the most psychologically flexible thing you can do is eat lunch.

2. Name the incident. Get very concrete: What specific thing triggered your annoyance?

Naming the incident brings you back to the present moment, with just the facts.

3. Notice the story. Ask yourself: What is my mind adding?

You do not have to reframe the story. Just see it as a story.

4. Ask, What is actually threatened? Often annoyance is organized around a perceived threat to control, comfort, being respected or being seen, or to resources and time.

When you can name the threat, you tend directly to it.

5. Open the aperture. Let the annoying thing be there, but widen your attention. Feel your feet, notice the room, notice another person’s face.

Notice that there is more here than this one irritation.

6. Choose connection where possible. Connection is anti-inflammatory. Instead of blaming and fixing and complaining when you are annoyed, try making contact with another person.

When You Are Annoyed, Remember This

Annoyance is a window that shows us where our capacity is low and where our mind is turning an incident into a story.

So this week, when annoyance shows up, see if you can pause before the complaint, check your body, and tend to your capacity. Then drop the story. So, you are stuck in an airport. What is the wise next best move?

For a deeper dive into this topic, listen to my podcast episode on annoyance, and the meditation that goes with it.

item.title: 3 Ways Snowplow Parenting Blocks Your Kid's Development
item.description:
Learned Helplessness

3 Ways Snowplow Parenting Blocks Your Kid's Development

Unmanaged parental protectiveness can actually cause more harm than the world.

Posted November 5, 2026

Key points
  • Snowplow parenting is a meticulous effort by parents to clear obstacles from their children’s lives.
  • The lack of autonomy under snowplow parenting hinders the development of a strong sense of self.
  • Parents must balance providing support and allowing their children space to learn, grow, and face challenges.
Source: Nicola Barts / Pexels

Diverging from the hands-off approach of laissez-faire parenting or the well-intentioned but hovering tendencies of helicopter parenting, "snowplow parenting" is characterized by a meticulous effort on the part of parents to clear away obstacles from their children’s lives. The manifestations are diverse, ranging from restricting age-appropriate activities to completing homework for the child, intervening in disagreements, and micromanaging the child’s daily life.

Parents who adopt a snowplow approach may find themselves doing everything for their children, rationalizing efficiency over independence. Excessive protective measures may manifest as an overbearing shield, preventing children from engaging in age-appropriate activities due to parental fear. This also extends to unilaterally clearing obstacles from their children’s paths and shielding them from the natural consequences of their actions.

While this may stem from well-intentioned roots of love and a shared aspiration for their child’s happiness and success, this style of parenting, rooted in overprotection, may inadvertently compromise children’s long-term well-being. It disrupts the delicate balance between support and independence, hindering the healthy development of crucial life skills.

Here are three ways snowplow parenting impacts kids as they transition into adulthood.

1. Lack of Autonomy

When parents consistently remove obstacles and make decisions for their children, the child is deprived of the opportunity to learn essential life skills and independence. The absence of autonomy becomes a pervasive theme in the lives of individuals raised under the shadow of snowplow parenting, influencing their self-perception and ability to navigate the world with resilience and confidence.

A study published in Emerging Adulthood underscores this point, shedding light on the impact of autonomy-restricting behaviors exhibited by parents during early adolescence. For instance, enforcing strict rules and curfews, micromanaging academic choices, and intervening in conflict resolution were found to have a pronounced effect on limiting teenagers’ independence and decision-making skills. Strikingly, these behaviors during early adolescence predicted a greater likelihood of parental dependence in emerging adulthood.

article continues after advertisement

The lack of autonomy under snowplow parenting hinders the development of a strong sense of self. Children raised in this environment may struggle to form their identities and make independent decisions as they enter adolescence and adulthood. Conditioned to rely on external guidance, they may grapple with self-doubt and challenges in asserting their individuality. This deficit in autonomy not only affects their ability to navigate life’s complexities but also diminishes confidence in their abilities, potentially impacting their mental health throughout their lives.

2. Learned Helplessness

The consistent intervention and obstacle-clearing actions of parents following this parenting style send a powerful message to the child—that challenges and obstacles are insurmountable without external aid. This belief, internalized during formative years, can persist into adulthood, impacting the individual’s confidence, motivation, and overall mental well-being.

One study highlighted how parental psychological control negatively affects students’ sense of control over academic success and contributes to learned helplessness. For example, when parents heavily dictate study habits, select courses, and micromanage every aspect of their child’s education, it diminishes the student’s agency. This fosters the belief that their efforts have minimal impact on academic outcomes, potentially leading to decreased motivation and a sense of resignation in their academic pursuits.

This learned helplessness can manifest in various aspects of their lives, affecting their professional endeavors, interpersonal relationships, and personal development. The lack of initiative cultivated during childhood may translate into a reluctance to take risks or pursue goals, hindering the fulfillment of their potential. The absence of early experiences in overcoming adversity can leave them ill-equipped to cope with the inevitable setbacks and hardships that life presents.

3. Difficulty Regulating Emotions

Emotional resilience, a pivotal aspect of mental health, evolves through experiencing and effectively coping with a range of emotions. Snowplow parenting, however, inadvertently impedes this growth by shielding children from life’s fluctuations. Individuals raised in such environments may encounter challenges in regulating their emotions in adulthood, struggling to navigate the complexities of their feelings and interpersonal relationships.

article continues after advertisement

Building upon these observations, a comprehensive review of research highlights a significant correlation between observed parental control during parent-child interactions and the prevalence of shyness and child anxiety disorders.

Moreover, when parents, fueled by anxiety, consistently remove obstacles and proactively address potential difficulties, they inadvertently transmit a heightened sense of apprehension to their children. This transmitted anxiety can significantly shape the child's worldview, impacting their confidence in confronting challenging situations.

While the intentions of snowplow parents come from a good place, the long-term impact on mental health cannot be overlooked. Lack of autonomy, learned helplessness, and difficulty regulating emotions are just a few of the potential consequences. It is essential for parents to strike a balance between providing support and allowing their children the space to learn, grow, and face life’s challenges on their own.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.com.

item.title: If You and Your Child Are More Nervous These Days, Here's What to Do
item.description:
Parenting

If You and Your Child Are More Nervous These Days, Here's What to Do

Three guideposts to help you get through anxious times.

Posted November 5, 2026

Key points
  • You can take an active role in navigating your nervousness and that of your child by modeling 3 guideposts.
  • Focus on controlling what you can control. Then you can have an impact on things that are indeed changeable.
  • Children of any age can learn from you that overwhelming things can be responded to.

These are difficult days for just about everyone. It is common for people coming to us to note that they are feeling more uneasy and that everyone they know is too. Parents are struggling with issues from financial insecurity to political unrest to safety concerns amid news reports of shootings and teen suicides. They are also seeing that the baseline level of anxiety in their children is at an all-time high, and this only exacerbates their own worrying.

How can you manage your feelings and those of your child? We have 3 guideposts to support you through these times. We suggest you talk with your child and model these as ways to work with what feels overwhelming to them. You are conveying that being upset is something we work with rather than something that's unchangeable. You can do this even with young children, varying the specific language to the child’s age.

1. Recognize what you can versus what you cannot control. There is an old saying: If you can change something, why worry? And if you can’t change it, why worry? Understanding that we cannot always change what happens to us but that we do have it within our power to change how we respond to it shifts us into more adaptive reactions. When we face challenges, we can look for what within the situation we can impact rather than just letting it loop anxiously in our minds. For example, we can become active in support of a political cause, get a second opinion about a medical problem, or, if it's a concern your child has in school, arrange a parent-teacher meeting.

2. Stop believing everything you think. We know this may seem like unexpected guidance from two professionals who focus on how people think and feel. It makes sense, however, when we recognize that anxiety is fungible–even if you have a positive impact on one thing that is troubling you, an anxious mind will look around for what else it needs to worry about. And our anxious minds are creative! There is always something nervousness can attach to in our lives, whether or not it may actually deserve significant concern. Recognizing that, we can get some perspective on automatic thoughts and that in and of itself is calming. If you name it, you tame it. With your child, you can identify the good outcomes that might be possible to widen the lens on what they foresee.

3. Learn what your body does when you are anxious. Our bodies express our feelings and if we focus on our bodies (“drop down into your body” ) rather than just our thoughts, we can actually do things to calm a nervous response. A calmer body signals to our minds that we are not as threatened as we might think we are. The first step is to identify where in your body anxiety tends to sit: Is it a churning belly or hunched shoulders or shallow breathing? Every person, adult or child, has their own characteristic body response to anxiety. If you know yours and you help your child identify theirs, you can work with it. There are many ways to do that. Deep slow breathing helps calm all areas of the body. There are relaxation techniques such as tensing all of our muscles on purpose—especially those hunched shoulders—and then unclenching all over. If you do this several times, your body learns that it doesn’t need to be so tense. In a sense, you are teaching your mind to stay with this moment, the one you are in right then, to draw your thoughts away from rehashing the past or predicting future catastrophes. Other common options to relax your body as your anxious thoughts swirl include meditation, journaling, listening to calming music, reaching out to a supportive person you trust such as a friend, family member, clergy member, or therapist. Getting out in nature is good to do as well. You and/or your child can do any or all of these things.

article continues after advertisement

Some anxiety is inevitable at times for just about all of us. The goal is to recognize it, name it as such, and begin to access ways to work with it as a malleable experience. We live in an uncertain world, and constant news and social media feeds can exacerbate our sense of vulnerability and impending doom. You can’t change everything that you find disturbing but you can use these tools to help you and your child feel more grounded and calm.

item.title: How Wisdom Helps Us Weather Life's Storms
item.description:
Wisdom

How Wisdom Helps Us Weather Life's Storms

Why we handle adversity better as we age.

Posted November 5, 2026

Key points
  • Remember what you have already survived.
  • Distinguish between what you can and cannot control.
  • Allow yourself to lean on others.
  • Make room for experiences that restore you.

As we get older, life has a way of testing us. We experience losses, disappointments, health scares and illness, changes in relationships, professional uncertainties, and the painful realization that often not everything in our lives will unfold as we had imagined. Adversity does not politely step aside as we enter the second half of life. In fact, some of life's most difficult challenges arrive when we might have expected to be more settled. And yet, something interesting happens as we age: We often become better equipped to face these challenges.

This is not because we are less vulnerable, or because difficult experiences hurt any less, but rather because we have developed a skill that can be enormously protective: perspective. Perspective allows us to understand that a difficult moment is not necessarily a permanent position.

We begin to understand that a difficult moment is not necessarily a permanent state.

When we are younger, adversity often feels all-consuming. A professional setback, a relationship ending, or a personal disappointment may feel like it threatens our entire future. This is often due to a lack of internal evidence and lived experience showing us that things can change for the better, that pain can and will soften, and that life can surprise us again.

With age comes a different type of knowledge. We have lived through difficult periods before. We have experienced moments we perhaps weren't sure how we would manage, and then disocvered that we did live through them. We have watched circumstances shift, relationships evolve and change, and seemingly unsurmountable problems become more manageable with time.

These invaluable experiences become part of our emotional psychological inheritance. They remind us that we have survived uncertainty before.

Experience teaches us what deserves our energy.

One of the gifts of growing older is becoming more discerning. We may spend less time trying to control what is truly beyond our control and more time focusing on the things we can influence. In doing so, we come to understand that not every disagreement requires a resolution, not every disappointment requires an explanation, and not every relationship can or should be repaired. We become more aware of where our energy is going and whether it is being invested in something meaningful.

The second half of life offers us the opportunity to cultivate a different kind of strength.

One of the greatest advantages to growing older is that we have a larger emotional landscape from which to draw. We have learned that life can be painful and beautiful, sometimes simultaneously. We understand that happiness is not a permanent state and that hardship does not define a life.

We become better at holding two truths at once: Something can be genuinely difficult and we can still find reasons for hope.

While experience can give us invaluable perspective, coping with adversity still requires intention and daily practice. Here are four ways to draw on the wisdom that comes with age:

  1. Remember what you have already survived. Think about the times you felt overwhelmed, uncertain, or afraid, but eventually found a way through. Reminding ourselves of our own resilience can help us restore a sense of confidence when circumstances feel scary or beyond our control.
  2. Distinguish between what you can and cannot control. Adversity often brings a desire to regain control. We may find ourselves repeatedly resisting conversations, worrying about outcomes, or trying to anticipate every possible scenario. Instead, focus your energy on what you can actually influence: the decisions you make, the boundaries you establish, and how you care for yourself. Learning to tolerate uncertainty is an important element of wisdom.
  3. Allow yourself to lean on others. Reach out to trusted friends, family members, or a therapist. Sharing our concerns can help us feel less isolated and offer perspectives we may not have thought of when caught up in our own worries. Connection is not a weakness but an important psychological resource.
  4. Make room for experiences that restore you. Make a conscious effort to continue doing things that bring pleasure, meaning, and a sense of connection. For me, this would be walking in nature, exercising, reading, and spending time with friends and family. For others it might mean painting, writing, or dancing. Although these activities won't make the problem go disappear, they remind us that our lives are bigger than the challenges we face.

item.title: Happy for You, Sad for Me
item.description:
Infertility

Happy for You, Sad for Me

Jealousy during infertility can reflect grief; self-compassion can ease the pain.

Posted November 5, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows that infertility can trigger painful social comparisons, envy, and feelings of isolation.
  • Jealousy over another person's pregnancy often reflects grief and longing rather than resentment.
  • Setting healthy boundaries can protect emotional well-being without sacrificing relationships.
  • Self-compassion and social support can help reduce shame and promote well-being during infertility.

If you’re struggling with infertility, you’ve likely experienced the pit-in-your-stomach sensation when someone close to you announces a pregnancy. You may simultaneously feel authentic joy for her and overwhelming grief for yourself. That sadness may turn to feelings of jealousy, anger, or even spite. While you don’t want anything horrible to happen to her, you may have fleeting thoughts of their pregnancy not working out. And then comes the guilt and self-doubt, asking yourself questions such as Am I a terrible person for having these thoughts?, What kind of friend am I?, and Why can't I just be happy for her?

Research shows that women struggling with infertility consistently experience envy of pregnant women and women with children, painful reactions to the pregnancies of friends and family members, negative self-comparisons, and withdrawal from situations that serve as reminders of their own struggles to conceive (Aiello et al., 2025).

Understanding what triggers these reactions can help you manage them with less guilt and without compromising your relationships or emotional well-being.

You Can Feel Two Things at Once

Give yourself permission to have two contradictory feelings at the same time. Being happy for someone else and feeling sad for yourself are not mutually exclusive. You can love your friend, want the very best for her, and still feel devastated by her pregnancy announcement. Often, it’s not really about her pregnancy at all, but rather a painful reminder of what you so desperately want and have invested so much of your time, energy, money, and hope into achieving.

The inability to be unconditionally supportive doesn't mean you're selfish or that you're not a good friend. It simply means you’re going through a devastating period in your life and that you want to experience the same joy as she gets to have.

When Everyone Else Seems to Be Moving Forward

It's natural to compare yourself with other people, particularly when they're reaching milestones you had hoped to achieve. During infertility, those comparisons can become difficult to escape when you are surrounded by pregnancy announcements, baby showers, first birthdays, and family photos. Staying connected to friends can be difficult when all they seem to talk about is their children, complain about sleepless nights, or announce they're expecting another baby. In fact, research shows that painful reminders, envy, negative self-comparison, and feelings of social exclusion and isolation are recurring themes in women's experiences of infertility (Aiello et al., 2025).

The hardest part may be the feeling that you are being left behind while everyone else's lives are moving forward. You may find that you start to measure your own losses against their milestones, remembering that a friend first got pregnant when you started your first IVF cycle or that another friend announced being pregnant with her second child as you were experiencing a pregnancy loss from a third transfer.

article continues after advertisement

These comparisons can be particularly painful because infertility involves so much uncertainty. There's often no clear timeline, no guarantee of success, and very little control over the outcome.

Feeling Jealous Doesn't Make You a Bad Person

Jealousy and envy are emotions most would rather not admit to experiencing because we want to think of ourselves as loving, generous, and supportive. Feeling jealous often leads to shame and self-loathing, which only compounds an already difficult life crisis.

But jealousy during infertility often has much more to do with your own sadness and disappointment than with resentment toward someone else. Infertility involves losses that aren't always visible or acknowledged by others. These intangible losses include an imagined timeline, the expectation of conceiving easily, or the sense of control you once had over your reproductive future.

Self-Protection Is Not Selfish

You don't have to put yourself in a painful situation to show support or prove you're happy for someone else. You can skip a baby shower, avoid a family gathering, or mute someone's pregnancy updates on social media. And you don't have to explain or justify every one of these decisions.

There are ways to be supportive while also taking care of yourself: You can send a thoughtful card or gift without attending the baby shower. You can congratulate a friend and let her know that while you're happy for her, you may need a little space to navigate your own struggles. You can take a break from social media or leave a gathering early if it becomes overwhelming.

Research suggests that social withdrawal and feelings of being misunderstood are common experiences during infertility (Aiello et al., 2025). While avoiding certain situations may provide temporary relief, losing connections with people who care about you and have good intentions can make the infertility experience even lonelier.

article continues after advertisement

Try to maintain relationships in which you feel understood and supported. That might mean spending time with friends who are sensitive to what you're going through, connecting with others experiencing infertility, joining a support group, or working with a mental health professional who understands reproductive mental health.

Show Yourself the Same Compassion You'd Give a Friend

Imagine that a close friend who's just been through her fourth unsuccessful IVF cycle tells you that her sister, who wasn’t even trying to conceive, announced she's pregnant—and now she wants nothing to do with her. You probably wouldn't tell her that she's a horrible person for feeling this way. Instead, you would recognize how complicated the situation is, how much she's been through, and how painful this news might be for her.

Self-compassion means extending some of that same kindness and understanding to yourself. And research suggests that self-compassion matters. In a study of women undergoing infertility treatment, self-compassion was one of the pathways that contributed to psychological well-being (Chu et al., 2021).

So next time you want to berate yourself for having thoughts and feelings that feel negative, remind yourself that it's understandable to have a difficult reaction to something you've wanted so badly and recognize that you can care deeply about someone and still feel sad about your own circumstances. Sometimes it simply means allowing yourself to feel disappointed without judging yourself for it.

Happy for You, Sad for Me

One of the hardest things about infertility is learning to live with emotions that don't always seem to fit together. You can feel hopeful and afraid, grateful and jealous, optimistic and discouraged. You can love the people around you and still find certain moments with them painful.

article continues after advertisement

The next time someone announces a pregnancy and you find yourself struggling with a mixture of happiness, jealousy, sadness, and guilt, know that it’s a completely normal reaction to a difficult situation and try not to judge yourself. You can be happy for other people and acknowledge your own sadness at the same time. Sometimes, allowing yourself to feel what you feel, without adding guilt or shame, can make a difficult experience a little easier.

item.title: A Fun Way to Build Relational Skills
item.description:
Relationships

A Fun Way to Build Relational Skills

Enjoyable stories can help us improve our relationships.

Posted November 5, 2026

Key points
  • Every story teaches us how to relate, for better or worse.
  • Enaging with fiction is an enjoyable way to build relational skills, even for people who don’t like self-help.
  • Novels, films, and series can bring the lessons of research and therapy to life.
  • Reflection and discussion questions turn enjoyable stories into tools for learning.

Our relationships are the source of some of our greatest joys and deepest pain. When our relationships are thriving, we tend to thrive, and when they’re strained, we suffer. In fact, many of the most pressing problems, not only in our personal lives but also in the larger world, such as interpersonal abuse, war, racism, climate change, and animal exploitation, are driven by dysfunctional ways of relating: to other people, to animals and the environment, and even to ourselves. So building relational literacy—the understanding of and ability to practice healthy ways of relating—can help transform these problems.

Yet the people who most need to build relational literacy are also probably the least likely to pick up a self-help book or go to therapy. They may, however, happily spend an evening engrossed in a novel or bingeing on Netflix.

What if we could build relational skills through reading or watching enjoyable stories?

Every Story Is Teaching Us How to Relate

Stories, whether written or on-screen, teach us things, from how a courtroom works to what healthy communication looks like. Research suggests that stories also shape our beliefs and attitudes, for better or worse. And because every story features characters, and characters are always relating—to others, and at the very least to themselves—every story is teaching us how to relate. The only question is whether we’re learning skillful or harmful ways of relating.

Consider the all-too-common bar scene in which an affronted man “communicates with his fists” by beating up a stranger who was making eyes at his partner. Or the many revenge movies in which an aggrieved parent (often a father) seeks not only to catch, but to brutalize, the person who kidnapped their child. In contrast, series like This Is Us portray complex relationships and characters who are nuanced and vulnerable, who turn toward rather than against or away from each other, and who repair after a relational breach.

Stories can also help us recognize difficult-to-identify dynamics, such as those that arise with addiction or domestic abuse. We often see more clearly when we look at a situation from the outside, as observers of someone else’s experience. For example, the film When a Man Loves a Woman reveals how alcohol dependence impacts a family system, while the novel and movie It Ends With Us reveal how gaslighting and trauma bonding operate in an abusive relationship.

Stories Bring Relational Lessons to Life

If you’re building relational skills through such means as reading nonfiction or taking courses, fiction can be a powerful supplement. Stories can bring the principles and tools described in nonfiction to life, showing what they look like and how they can be applied. This is why, after writing seven nonfiction books, several of which are about relationships, I wrote a novel. I wanted readers to be able to see relational concepts in action while also being entertained.

Questions to Help You Put Stories’ Lessons Into Practice

To get more out of novels and shows as tools for relational learning, you can use a list of questions for post-reading or -viewing. You can tailor the list to areas you want to grow in or concepts you’re learning through therapy or nonfiction (for example, attachment styles, relational repair, or the Gottmans’ “four horsemen”), and use it for personal reflection or for discussion with someone you’ve read or watched with.

You can start with questions like the following:

  • What attachment styles did the characters seem to have (for example, secure or anxious)?
  • Did you see any of the four horsemen being used (criticism, contempt, defensiveness, stonewalling)? What could the characters have done instead?
  • What are some examples of characters turning toward each other? What are some examples of them turning against or away from each other?
  • In what ways were conflict or disagreements handled skillfully?
  • In what ways were conflict or disagreements handled unskillfully, and what could have been done differently?
  • Overall, did the characters seem to relate in a way that fosters security and connection, or insecurity and disconnection?
  • How do the characters’ experiences apply to your own situation?

I’ve always believed that a great story leaves the reader or viewer a little better off than they were before. Whether you’re a therapist working with clients or an individual wanting to build your relational skills, consider adding stories to your relational toolkit. Stories not only teach us; they can help us have fun in the process of learning.
